SECURITY.TXT CHECKER · RFC 9116 · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is your security.txt still valid — or quietly expired?

Paste a security.txt and check it against RFC 9116. The field that catches most sites is Expires: the RFC says data in an expired file must be considered stale, so once that date passes a conforming researcher treats your file as publishing no contact at all — while the server keeps serving it, nothing 404s, and it still reads fine to a human. Nothing about that failure is visible from the outside.

Nothing is uploaded. The text you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device — no small thing here, since a list of which companies someone is checking is itself sensitive.

1. Check a security.txt

2. Result

LineFieldValue

Findings

not checked here Where the file is served from, and the media type it is served with, cannot be seen from pasted text. Those two checks need the CLI below.

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

The CLI fetches the file over real HTTP, tries /.well-known/security.txt first and the legacy root copy second, and adds the two checks a paste cannot support — the served location and the media type: 

node check.mjs example.com
node check.mjs example.com --json
node check.mjs https://example.com/.well-known/security.txt --timeout 5000

Get check.mjs, engine.mjs and fetch-url.mjs from the repo — plain Node 18+, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the host you name; nothing goes through this site. Exit code 1 on a danger-severity finding or when no security.txt could be fetched at all, 0 otherwise.

This is the one check in this catalogue worth scheduling. Every other conformance rule here is stable once fixed — but Expires is a date, so a file that passes today fails on its own, with no commit and no deploy to blame. A monthly CI run is how you find out before a researcher does.

What's checked

CheckWhat it flagsSeverityNeeds the CLI?
ExpiredExpires is in the past — RFC 9116 says the whole file must then be treated as staleDangerNo
Expires missing / duplicated / malformedRFC 9116 requires exactly one, as an ISO 8601 timestampDangerNo
Expires too far out or nearly dueMore than a year ahead (the RFC recommends under a year), or under 30 days leftNoticeNo
Contact missing or not a URINo Contact at all, or a bare address rather than a mailto:/https:/tel: URIDangerNo
Insecure URIA Contact over plain http: (danger), or another field over http: (notice)Danger / NoticeNo
Key pasted into the fileA PGP key block inline, which RFC 9116 forbids — Encryption takes a URIDangerNo
Malformed lineA line that is neither Field: value, a # comment, nor blankDangerNo
Silently-ignored fieldAcknowledgements (the RFC spells it without the middle "e") and other unknown names a conforming parser dropsNoticeNo
Signed with no CanonicalA cleartext-signed file that does not say where it is meant to liveNoticeNo
Wrong locationServed from the site root rather than /.well-known/security.txtNoticeYes
Wrong media typeNot served as text/plain; charset=utf-8NoticeYes

More: why RFC 9116 made Expires mandatory, and what an expired file costs you. See also: how this differs from securitytxt.org's generator and validator, and where eyeballing a security.txt usually goes wrong.

Common questions

What does an expired security.txt actually break?

RFC 9116 says data in an expired file must be considered stale and should not be used. So once the Expires date passes, a conforming researcher or automated tool treats your file as if it published no contact at all — even though the server is still serving it and it still looks fine to a human reading it. Nothing goes red, nothing 404s, and the file quietly stops doing its job. That is why Expires is the field this tool checks first.

Why does Contact have to be a URI?

RFC 9116 defines Contact as a URI field so that a consumer can act on it without guessing what kind of thing it is. security@example.com could be an address or a username; mailto:security@example.com cannot be anything else. Write a web form as https:, an email address as mailto:, and a phone number as tel:. A bare address is the single most common conformance failure after the expiry date.

Where does the file have to live?

At /.well-known/security.txt. A copy at the site root is tolerated by some tooling for historical reasons, but conforming consumers look under /.well-known/ and will not find a root-only copy. The browser tool here cannot see where your file is served from — you pasted the text, not the URL — so that check is one the CLI does.

Is this a security assessment?

No. It checks whether one text file conforms to the rules RFC 9116 states about that file. It does not test the site, scan for vulnerabilities, verify that anyone reads the address you publish, or confirm that the people behind it respond. A perfectly conforming security.txt on an unmaintained inbox passes every check here.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal or security advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. It reports whether the text you provided satisfies specific, mechanically checkable rules from RFC 9116 — nothing more. It is not a security assessment, not a vulnerability scan, and not a determination that your disclosure process works. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get check.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything you paste runs in your browser and is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass over the same site: Security Headers Check classifies a page's CSP and clickjacking protection. AI Crawler Access Check checks whether your robots.txt allows the crawlers you think it does. Email Auth Check checks SPF, DKIM and DMARC for the domain your Contact address lives on.

vs-checking-it-by-eye.html.text:
← back to the checker

security.txt Checker vs. checking it by eye

This page names no specific product or company: "checking it by eye" is reading a security.txt file yourself, a generic habit anyone with a text editor already has, not a competing tool.

Reading a security.txt file and eyeballing it for problems genuinely catches the case everyone pictures: a file with no Contact field at all, or one that is completely empty. That case is real, and it is not what this tool exists to replace. What it replaces is everything past that — a field whose value is wrong in a way that still reads as ordinary, complete text to a person scanning the file.

Where eyeballing it usually goes wrong

CaseChecking it by eyeThis checker
Expires: 2025-06-01T00:00:00ZReads as an ordinary date sitting in a list of fields — nothing about its formatting changes whether it is next week or years pastCompares it against the actual current time and flags an expired file by name
Contact: security@example.comReads as an obviously correct contact address — it is oneFlags it as not a URI: RFC 9116 requires the mailto: prefix specifically, so a parser can tell what kind of contact it is
Acknowledgements: (British spelling)Reads as a completely ordinary field nameFlags the misspelling by name and names the RFC-correct spelling, Acknowledgments
Encryption: http://example.com/pgp-key.txtAn http vs. https difference of one letter, easy to skim past in a long URLFlags plain-http explicitly
Preferred-Languages: EnglishReads as a perfectly reasonable valueFlags that "English" is not a valid language tag — RFC 9116 wants a tag like en
Policy https://example.com/vulnerability-policy (no colon)Still reads as a complete, sensible line — a field name followed by a URLFlags it as a malformed field with the colon missing, since without it the line is not a field a parser can use at all

The gap that matters most: a wrong value can look exactly like a right one

Every case above shares the same shape: none of them looks broken. An expired date is still a date. A bare email address is still a contact. A misspelled field name is still a word. A missing colon still reads as a sentence. There is no red flag, no obviously wrong formatting — just a field whose meaning to a conforming parser differs from what it looks like to a person who already knows what the file is trying to say. This checker applies RFC 9116's own rules to every field, so a value that is wrong in a way invisible to a reader still gets flagged.

When to still read the file yourself

This is a conformance check, not a security review. It has no opinion on whether the contact address is actually monitored, whether the linked policy page is any good, or where the file is served from — a paste cannot show that, only the CLI checking a live URL can. Judging the substance behind the file is still a job for reading it.

Common questions

What does checking a security.txt by eye actually catch?

It catches the case everyone tests: a file with no Contact field at all, or an obviously empty file. That is real, and it is not what this tool exists to replace. What it replaces is everything past that — a field whose value is wrong in a way that still reads as ordinary text.

Why does eyeballing miss an expired Expires date?

A date sitting in a list of fields looks like a normal date whether it is next week or three years ago — nothing about its formatting changes when it is in the past. RFC 9116 says a consumer must treat an expired file's data as stale, so the file quietly stops doing its job while still looking complete to a person reading it. This checker compares the date against the actual current time and flags it by name.

Why does eyeballing miss a bare-address Contact?

security@example.com reads as an obviously correct contact address to a person — it is one. RFC 9116 requires Contact to be a URI specifically, so a conforming tool cannot tell whether that string is an email address, a username, or something else without the mailto: prefix. The distinction that matters to a parser is invisible to a reader who already knows what it means.

Why does eyeballing miss a misspelled field name?

Acknowledgements (the British spelling, with the extra e) reads as a completely normal word. RFC 9116 spells the field Acknowledgments, without it, and a conforming parser silently ignores any field name it does not recognize — so the misspelled field, and whatever page it points to, simply never gets found by anything that reads the file correctly, with no error and no visual cue.

Why does eyeballing miss a missing colon?

Policy https://example.com/vulnerability-policy without a colon after Policy still reads as a complete, sensible line — a field name followed by a URL. RFC 9116 requires the colon; without it, the line is not a field at all, just unstructured text a parser cannot use. It looks identical to a correct line at a glance.

Does this tool replace reading the file yourself?

No. It only checks conformance to RFC 9116's own rules about field syntax, required fields, and their formats — it has no opinion on whether the contact address is monitored, whether the policy page is any good, or whether the file is even reachable at the right location from a paste alone. Judging the substance is still a job for reading it.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It checks whether a security.txt file conforms to RFC 9116, not a security assessment of your site. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you paste, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use it as a system of record — nothing you paste is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything you paste runs in your browser and is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors.

Back to the checker

vs-securitytxt-org-generator.html.text:
← security.txt Checker

This tool vs. securitytxt.org's generator and validator

securitytxt.org is the reference site for the format — it is where most people first meet security.txt, and it offers a form that generates a file and a validator that checks one. If you do not have a security.txt yet, start there: filling in a form is a better way to produce a first file than reading an RFC.

This tool is aimed at a different moment. Not "help me write one", but "the one we wrote eighteen months ago — is it still doing anything?" Those turn out to want different shapes.

The difference in one sentence

A generator is used once. Expires is a date, so conformance is not a one-time state — which means the useful tool is the one you can put on a schedule and forget, rather than the one you have to remember to revisit.

securitytxt.orgThis tool
Main jobGenerate a conforming file, and validate one interactivelyRe-check a file you already publish, by hand or on a schedule
InterfaceWeb formWeb page and a zero-dependency Node CLI
Usable in CINot its purposeYes — exit code 1 on a must-fix finding
Fetches your live file—Yes: tries /.well-known/security.txt, then the legacy root copy
Checks the served location and media type—Yes, in CLI mode (a paste cannot show either)
Separates must-fix from worth-knowing—Yes: RFC MUSTs are dangers, SHOULDs and typos are notices
Runs without sending your file anywhere—Yes — browser-local, or your own machine via the CLI

The dashes are "not what that tool is for", not "does it badly". The two columns are also not a live feature audit: this page describes securitytxt.org from its well-known role as the format's reference site rather than from a fetch made while writing it, and a site can change. Check it yourself before treating the row as current — and if it now does the thing you need, use it.

When securitytxt.org is the better answer

  • You are publishing for the first time. A form that emits a correct file beats a checker that tells you the file you do not have is missing.
  • You want the canonical reading of the spec. It is the format's own site; this is a third-party checker with no special authority.
  • You want to sign the file interactively. Nothing here generates or signs keys — this tool only reads what you already have.

When this one is

  • You want to find out before a researcher does. An expired file serves a 200, reads correctly, and publishes nothing to a conforming consumer. Only a deliberate check catches that.
  • You want it automated. One scheduled job, no account, no form:
node check.mjs example.com   # exit 1 once Expires has passed
  • You manage more than one domain. A form is per-file; a CLI is a loop.
  • You would rather not paste it into a website at all. The browser page here never uploads what you type, and the CLI talks only to the host you name.

Using both is the sensible answer

Generate the file at securitytxt.org, publish it at /.well-known/security.txt, then put node check.mjs yourdomain.com on a monthly schedule so the expiry date stops being something you have to hold in your head. The two tools are not really competing; they cover the start and the middle of the same job.

Common questions

Should I use this or securitytxt.org?

If you do not have a security.txt yet, start at securitytxt.org: filling in a form is a better way to produce a first file than reading an RFC. Come back here for the question that arrives later, which is whether the file you already published is still doing anything. The two cover the start and the middle of the same job, and using both is the sensible answer.

Why does a security.txt need re-checking at all?

Because Expires is a date. A generator is used once, but RFC 9116 makes the expiry field mandatory and time-bound, so conformance is not a one-time state — which means the useful tool is the one you can put on a schedule and forget, rather than the one you have to remember to revisit.

When is securitytxt.org the better answer?

When you are publishing for the first time, since a form that emits a correct file beats a checker that tells you the file you do not have is missing. When you want the canonical reading of the spec, since it is the format's own site and this is a third-party checker with no special authority. And when you want to sign the file interactively, since nothing here generates or signs keys — this tool only reads what you already have.

Is this comparison a live feature audit?

No. This page describes securitytxt.org from its well-known role as the format's reference site rather than from a fetch made while writing it, and a site can change. Check it yourself before treating any row as current — and if it now does the thing you need, use it.

Back to the tool: security.txt Checker. Background: why RFC 9116 made Expires mandatory.

why-security-txt-expires.html.text:
← security.txt Checker

Why RFC 9116 made security.txt expire

Most conformance rules are static. You fix the file once, and it stays fixed until somebody edits it. Expires is not like that: it is a date, so a file that passes every check today fails on its own — with no commit, no deploy, and nothing in any log to point at. That is not an oversight in the specification. It is the specification's main idea.

The problem the field exists to solve

Before RFC 9116, the worst outcome for a published disclosure contact was not a missing file. It was an abandoned one. A security.txt published in 2019, naming an address that stopped being monitored in 2021, gives a researcher every reason to believe they have reached the right place — and no way at all to tell that they have not. They send the report, they wait, they hear nothing, and eventually they conclude you do not care. From your side, nothing happened, because nothing arrived.

A mandatory expiry date makes that staleness explicit. After the date, the file is no longer vouching for itself, and a consumer knows to stop trusting it rather than having to infer abandonment from silence.

What an expired file actually does

RFC 9116 states that data in an expired file must be considered stale and should not be used. So to a conforming researcher or automated consumer, an expired security.txt publishes nothing at all. A person holding a real finding falls back to whatever else they can find — a support form that routes to billing, a public issue tracker, a social post, or nobody.

Meanwhile: the server returns 200. The text still reads correctly to a human. Every uptime check, every link checker, and every deploy pipeline you have stays green. This failure has no symptom on your side, which is exactly why it is worth checking deliberately.

Choosing a value

The RFC recommends less than a year ahead. Two competing pressures decide where inside that range you land:

  • Shorter is a stronger claim. A date three months out says somebody looked at this recently. A date eleven months out says somebody wanted to not think about it.
  • But the date has to be one you will honour. A short expiry you forget is strictly worse than a long one you meant, because it lapses sooner.

The way out of that trade-off is not a cleverer date, it is automation. If a scheduled job checks the file, the expiry length stops being a bet on your own memory: 

node check.mjs example.com   # exit 1 once Expires has passed

That is the one check in this catalogue genuinely worth putting on a schedule rather than in a per-commit pipeline, because the thing that changes is the calendar, not the code.

The other silent failures

Expiry is the most common, but it shares a shape with the rest of the quiet ones: they are all legal-looking text that a conforming parser simply ignores.

Acknowledgements with the middle "e"

The RFC field is Acknowledgments. The British spelling is not a recognised field, and RFC 9116 says consumers must ignore fields they do not recognise — so the hall-of-fame page you are pointing at is simply never found. No error, no warning, nothing.

A bare address in Contact

Contact is defined as a URI field. security@example.com is not a URI; mailto:security@example.com is. A consumer that resolves URIs will skip the first one, and a human reading the file will not notice the difference.

A key pasted into the file

RFC 9116 is explicit that keys must not appear in security.txt — Encryption takes a URI that points at one. An inline PGP block also breaks the line-oriented format for every field after it, so it tends to take the rest of your file down with it.

A signed file with no Canonical

A cleartext signature proves the text is yours. It does not prove where the text was meant to live, so a signed file copied to another host verifies just as well. Canonical is what closes that gap, which is why the RFC says to use it when the file is signed.

Common questions

Why did RFC 9116 make Expires mandatory?

Because the failure mode the format had before it was an abandoned file that still looked authoritative. A security.txt published in 2019 naming an address that stopped being monitored in 2021 gives a researcher every reason to believe they have reached the right place, and no way to tell they have not. A mandatory expiry date makes staleness explicit rather than invisible: after that date, a conforming consumer knows the file is no longer vouched for, instead of guessing from a timestamp nobody publishes.

What does an expired file actually do?

RFC 9116 says data in an expired file must be considered stale and should not be used. In practice that means a conforming researcher or automated consumer treats you as publishing no disclosure contact — so a person holding a real finding falls back to whatever they can find: a support form, a public issue tracker, a social post, or nothing. The server keeps returning 200, the text still reads correctly to a human, and no monitoring you have will notice.

How long should Expires be?

RFC 9116 recommends less than a year into the future. A shorter value is a stronger claim — it says someone looked at this recently — and a very long one gives away most of the benefit, since the point is to force a periodic re-check rather than to be a formality. The practical answer is to pick a period you will actually honour and automate the renewal, because a date chosen to avoid maintenance is a date that will pass unnoticed.

What else silently fails in a security.txt?

The quiet ones share a shape: they are legal-looking text a conforming parser ignores. "Acknowledgements" with the middle e is not the RFC field name, so the page it points at is never found. A bare email address in Contact is not a URI, so a consumer that resolves URIs skips it. An unknown field name must be ignored by conforming parsers, per the RFC, so anything you invented does nothing. None of these produce an error anywhere — the file parses, serves, and under-delivers.

Check your own file: security.txt Checker. See also: how this differs from securitytxt.org's generator and validator.
